title: PPE for cleaning tasks: choosing, putting on and taking off
audience: Cleaning staff who work in patient areas, clinics and treatment rooms.
learningOutcomes: List the three factors used to decide which protective equipment is needed.
Put on protective equipment in the correct order.
Remove protective equipment in the order that avoids self-contamination.

instruction.heading: Choosing protective equipment
instruction.body: Select protective equipment through a task-specific assessment: estimate the chance of touching blood or other fluids, identify the fluid, and consider how the organism is likely to travel. Typical items are aprons, gowns, gloves, masks, goggles and visors, each needing a Therapeutic Goods Administration listing or recognised equivalent.

instruction.heading: When gloves are needed
instruction.body: Gloves are worn when direct contact is expected with blood, body fluid, mucous membranes or broken skin, or when touching kit or surfaces that look or might be contaminated. They do not reveal a needle puncture, so they never substitute for the sharps measures in “Sharps: handling, containers and injury response”. When donning a full set, gloves come last.

instruction.heading: Putting on
instruction.body: Start by washing your hands. Drape the gown from neck to knee and out to the wrists, wrap it round the back, and tie it at the neck and waist. Position the mask's straps at the crown and nape. Set goggles or a visor over the eyes and face and tighten it for fit. Gloves are the last layer and extend over the gown's cuffs.

instruction.heading: Taking off
instruction.body: Strip off at the threshold or in an anteroom. Begin with gloves, since their exterior is contaminated: grasp one glove's exterior with the other gloved hand and peel it away, hold it, slide a bare finger beneath the second glove's wrist and draw it inside out over the first. Wash your hands. Lift goggles by the strap or arms, as the lens is contaminated. Loosen the gown, draw it off the shoulders using only the inner side, turn it inside out, and roll it for disposal. Remove the mask by the ties, never touching its front. Wash your hands the moment everything is off.

instruction.heading: Respirators
instruction.body: A standard surgical mask may be lifted off where care is delivered. Removing a P2 respirator means washing hands, leaving the room, or entering an anteroom, placing the sealed respirator into a container and washing again. The guideline presents this as a footnote to the removal order.

procedure: Identify the task and the likely exposure before choosing the protective equipment.
Clean your hands, then put on the gown or apron, then the mask, then eye protection, then gloves.
Complete the task without touching your face or the front of any protective item.
At the doorway or anteroom, remove the gloves first, using the outer-surface method.
Clean your hands, remove eye protection, then the gown turned inside out, then the mask.
Clean your hands again immediately after the last item, and bin everything in the correct container.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner must clean a splash of body fluid on a patient room floor and a bedside rail.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which protective equipment is needed, and which item comes off first?
workedExamples.reasoning: Gloves are needed for the contact, and an apron or gown and eye protection are needed where splashing may occur. The gloves come off first at the doorway, because their outside is the most contaminated item, followed by hand cleaning.

equipmentAndPpe: Disposable gloves in the correct size
Apron or gown as the risk requires
P2 respirator only where the facility's risk assessment and the sequence require it

commonErrors.error: Removing the gown before the gloves.
commonErrors.prevention: Remove gloves first, clean hands, then remove the other items.

commonErrors.error: Touching the mask's front while lifting it off.
commonErrors.prevention: Hold the ties and dispose of the mask without touching the front.

commonErrors.error: Adjusting eye protection with contaminated gloves.
commonErrors.prevention: Take gloves off, clean hands, then handle eye protection by its strap or ear pieces.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Protective equipment is a final safeguard rather than a first line. Use it inside the task's risk review, along with cleaning, hand washing and safe sharps practice.
A P2 respirator needs the guideline's sequence, with hand cleaning and removal outside the room. Fit checks and training fall to the facility.
Hand hygiene comes before putting on protective equipment and immediately after removing it, every time.

qualityStandard: Learner chooses the correct items for a described task using the three factors.
Learner puts on the items in the correct order.
Learner removes the items in the correct order without contaminating the hands.
documentationEvidence: PPE selection record for the task
Record of any exposure incident and the referral
summary: Choose protective equipment from the exposure, the body substance and the transmission route.
Put on in order: hand hygiene, gown, mask, eye protection, gloves.
Remove gloves first, then clean hands, then eye protection, gown and mask, then clean hands again.

knowledgeChecks.question: What are the three factors the guideline gives for choosing protective equipment?
options: The cost, the colour and the brand, and the size of the packet and the box
How likely exposure is, the kind of body fluid involved, and the likely spread route.
The shift length, the room number and the supervisor's name, and the bin the gloves go in
The weather, the time of day and the number of visitors, and the colour of the mop head

knowledgeChecks.question: Which item comes off first after a cleaning task?
options: The mask, pulled down to the chin first
The gown, unfastened at the neck first
The gloves, using the outer-surface method.
The eye protection, lifted off first.

knowledgeChecks.question: Where should protective equipment be removed?
options: In the corridor outside the building.
At the doorway or in an anteroom.

Source priority: the NHMRC guideline is an official Australian source. Where it conflicts with informal or in-house cleaning advice, the guideline governs the points this lesson relies on.

Australian Guidelines for Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare, edition note: the 2019 edition is the current edition (NHMRC, https://www.safetyandquality.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-05/australian-guidelines-for-the-prevention-and-control-of-infection-in-healthcare.pdf; CONFIRMED in the figures register, checked 2026-11-02); the uploaded copy read on 2026-11-02 is the 2010 edition, so points taken from it are UNCONFIRMED against the 2019 text.
